newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Roadblocks, sporadic violence keep Albania tense.
newsitem.headline: Roadblocks, sporadic violence keep Albania tense.

text.p: Sporadic violence, anti-government demonstrations in several towns and a blockade of the main north-south road kept tensions high in crisis-hit Albania on Friday.
A teenager was stabbed during the 10th day of protests in the seaside town of Vlore, 150 km (85 miles) south of the capital Tirana. Three people were killed during clashes in Vlore earlier this week.
Witnesses said Adnan Gjoni, 17, was stabbed in the neck and shoulder after accusing a man in the crowd of being a secret policeman. He was in hospital but out of danger.
Scuffles broke out in Fier, also south of Tirana, when 100 riot police tried to keep several thousand protesters from the town's square and hall. The hall was burned during clashes last month.
Protesters, enraged after men attacked a demonstration on Thursday, threw stones at police trying to keep them from the square. Police quickly gave ground, leaving an uneasy calm.
About 5,000 people demonstrated in Fier and 7,000 in Vlore. Both groups chanted: "Down with (President Sali) Berisha", "We want our money back" and "Thieves, thieves".

Protesters erected three barricades on the north-south road between Fier and Vlore, cutting the main landlink between the country's second port and the capital. At one of the roadblocks two truckloads of gravel where dumped on the highway.
Several hundred demonstrators in the southern town of Gjirokaster lit candles in the evening and formed the word "Vlore" in a show of solidarity.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been swept for the past month by protests and riots by investors who lost their life savings in failed high-risk investment schemes.
The schemes lured new money with offers of high interest rates and then used the cash to pay earlier investors. A large proportion of Albania's adults seem to have joined the schemes.
Investors now blame Berisha's ruling Democratic Party for letting the schemes flourish and opposition parties accuse him of using cash from the schemes to finance an election campaign last year.

The government, in turn, says opposition groups are trying to exploit the crisis. It impounded about $300 million from two failed funds but steadfastly refused to use government money to reimburse luckless investors.
The main opposition Forum for Democracy snubbed Tritan Shehu, Democratic Party chairman and deputy prime minister, by refusing to attend all-party talks to discuss the crisis.
Five smaller right-wing parties attended and demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government.

"The only concrete solution is the resignation of the government which the people no longer believe in," said Hysen Selfo, leader of the National Front Party which has three seats in the 140-member parliament.
Meksi's government appears determined to weather the crisis but diplomats say the scale of the economic collapse could be enormous.

After the meeting, Shehu blamed the protests and violence on the main Forum opposition parties, accusing them of "terrorist acts and political manipulation of the people and politically exploiting a fabricated situation".
Some estimates put the losses from the collapsed schemes at $2 billion, about the size of Albania's annual gross domestic product. Five national schemes have now gone officially bust.
Four more companies, which deny they are pyramids and say they are corporate holdings, have drastically cut back their interest payments and have frozen depositors' assets.
Leaders of the Forum for Democracy said Berisha was pushing the country to civil war and called for worldwide support to stop any acts of violence or intimidation.
"We declare that in the situation where the government is taking Albania to a civil war, we are unprotected," Kurt Kola, the head of the Forum, said in a statement.
